title: Rep. Jack K. Daniels voted Yea on HB667, a public safety and offender monitoring bill
text:
Rep. Jack K. Daniels voted Yea on HB667, a public safety and offender monitoring bill
Rep. Jack K. Daniels (R-32nd) voted Yea on HB667, a public safety and offender monitoring bill, which passed the Ohio House 96-2 during the 136th Ohio General Assembly on Wednesday, June 10, 2026, according to the Ohio Legislature.
The following summary and breakdown are based on the bill's official text and may include interpretation to clarify the bill's provisions.
This bill, known as the Reagan Tokes and Patrick Heringer Act, requires certain felony-related and escape warrants, including those involving high-risk offenders, to be entered into the LEADS and NCIC databases within 48 hours and removed within 48 hours after service, recall or error discovery, with 24/7 nationwide extradition for specified offenses. It mandates GPS monitoring for certain released offenders using a single statewide vendor, with inclusion and exclusion zones, continuous tracking, and crime scene correlation tools that give local law enforcement real-time, warrantless access to location and related crime data. The bill also refines targeted community alternatives to prison rules and clarifies sentencing and procedural cross-references.
HB667 was introduced by Rep. Cindy Abrams.
Daniels is serving his first term in the Ohio House of Representatives after being appointed in 2024. He represents the 32nd House District and holds additional roles as Vice Chair of the House Transportation Committee and member of the Insurance, Small Business, and Ways and Means committees.
Daniels has a background in business, having attended the University of Akron and founded multiple companies in the trucking industry.
He began his public service career on the Portage Lakes Career Center School Board, later winning an at-large seat on the New Franklin City Council in 2021, and became Council President in 2024.
In Ohio, the legislative process begins when a bill is introduced in either the House of Representatives or the Senate. A bill must receive three considerations in each chamber, and it may be referred to a committee for hearings, debate and possible amendments before advancing to a floor vote. If both chambers pass the same version, the bill is sent to the governor, who can sign it, veto it or allow it to become law without a signature. The Ohio General Assembly begins a new legislative session every two years on the first Monday in January of odd-numbered years, and there is no limit on the number of days it may convene.
